math_verification: All problem answers hand-verified in problem_spec.verification.

design_principles.principle: Every statistic gets an error bar
design_principles.app_approach: The lecture opens with a Sharpe-ratio confidence-interval calculator: same point estimate, different reliability, computed live.

design_principles.principle: The hurdle is a function of N
design_principles.app_approach: A Bonferroni slider makes the central HLZ claim tactile: at one test t=1.96 means something; at 316 it means nothing.
HLZ, McLean–Pontiff, Hou–Xue–Zhang, JKP, and Chen–Welch are staged as a courtroom sequence ending in the four-criteria gauntlet that value and momentum survive.

blocks.block_title: Every Backtest Is a Random Variable

slides.title: The Best-Looking Backtest Is the Most Overfit
slides.content_summary: Sample Sharpe ratios are random variables, so screens select noise (Type I) and discard real signals (Type II) — the more you try, the worse. Optimization exaggerates it: weights chase the largest, noisiest in-sample means. The disciplines: track everything tried (rejected signals are the denominator of every honest correction), declare signs ex ante, never use full-sample moments, simulate what pure noise would produce.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why does the significance screen guarantee the discovered signals are biased upward even when some are real?'

slides.title: Same Sharpe, Different Reliability
slides.content_summary: SE(SR̂) = √[(1/(T−1))(1+SR²/2)] under normal iid; higher moments enter for real strategies: (1+SR²·kurt/4−SR·skew). Worked pair: both SR 0.80 over T=60 months — symmetric A has SE 0.46, insurance-seller B (skew −3.1, kurt 19.9) has SE 0.63, 38% wider; P(SR̂<0) is 4.1% vs 10.3%. Jackknife beats bootstrap with outliers. Report the interval, the ±3σ count, and the fraction of months carrying the result.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why does taking a RATIO of two mismeasured numbers make the interval wider than either input\'s?'

slides.title: Your Turn: Put an Error Bar on a Sharpe

problem_spec.scenario: A backtest reports SR̂ = 0.5 over T = 120 observations. Under normal iid returns, SE = √[(1/(T−1))(1 + SR̂²/2)] and the 95% CI is SR̂ ± 2·SE (the deck's formula card, plugging SR̂ directly).
problem_spec.verification: 1 + 0.5²/2 = 1.125; /119 = 0.0094538; √ = 0.0972. CI lower bound = 0.5 − 2×0.0972 = 0.5 − 0.1945 = 0.3055 ≈ 0.31. A decade of data cannot statistically separate a 0.5-Sharpe strategy from a 0.31 one — or from a 0.69 one.

slides.title: What 316 Factors Do to t = 2
slides.content_summary: HLZ: 313 papers, 316 published factors — an undercount, since discarded factors are unobservable and journals publish discoveries, not replications. The published record is the right tail of everything tried. Bonferroni hurdle t = Φ⁻¹(1−0.05/2N): 1.96 at one test, 3.09 at 25, 3.28 at 50, 3.48 at 100, 4.06 at 1000; the projection reaches ≈4.0/3.8/3.4 (Bonf/Holm/BHY) by 2032. A t of 2.0 in this literature is the expected best draw from noise.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why does the hurdle climb so slowly — 100 tests to 1000 moves it only 3.48 to 4.06?'

slides.title: Three Corrections, Three Verdicts
slides.content_summary: FWER = P(any false discovery) vs FDR = expected false fraction. Bonferroni p ≤ α/M (flat, harshest); Holm p(i) ≤ α/(M−i+1) (step-down, convex); BHY p(i) ≤ (i/M)·α/c(M) (linear, FDR, valid under dependence). HLZ's worked ten tests: 10 / 3 / 4 / 6 discoveries. Applied to the literature: of 296 significant factors, 158 (Bonf), 142 (Holm), 132 (BHY) are false — the conclusion doesn't depend on the method.

slides.title: Your Turn: Set the Honest Hurdle

problem_spec.scenario: A desk has tested N = 100 signals this year and wants a 5% family-wise error rate using Bonferroni. (Useful: Φ⁻¹(1 − 0.00025) = 3.48.)
problem_spec.verification: Per-test p = 0.05/100 = 0.0005 = 0.05%. Two-sided t hurdle = Φ⁻¹(1 − 0.0005/2) = Φ⁻¹(0.99975) = 3.48 (the deck's own N=100 point). The 1.96 bar was used up by the 99 other signals.

blocks.block_title: Out of Sample: The Decay and Its Anatomy

slides.title: Publication Kills (Some of) the Predictor
slides.content_summary: McLean–Pontiff, 97 predictors: mean return 0.582%/mo in sample → 0.402 out of sample → 0.264 post publication. Headline decomposition: −26% is statistical bias (would happen if nobody read the paper), a further −32% is publication-informed trading. The mechanism is visible: trading volume and short−long short interest roughly DOUBLE post-publication (0.092→0.187; 0.166→0.315, p=0.000). Decay is largest for price-only, cheap-to-arbitrage predictors; 12 of 97 never replicated at all.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why is the post-publication drop evidence about MISPRICING rather than risk? What would a risk premium do at the publication date?'

problem_spec.scenario: McLean & Pontiff estimate returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower post publication (both relative to in-sample).
problem_spec.verification: Publication-informed trading = 58 − 26 = 32 points. Share of the total post-publication decay attributable to trading = 32/58 = 55.2%. Slightly more than half the decay is the market learning; the rest was never real.

slides.title: The Bayesian Rebuttal (Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen)
slides.content_summary: JKP re-run the crisis with one uniform recipe: 153 factors, 93 countries, open-sourced. Seven bars: 35.0 (HXZ raw) → 55.6 (construction) → 61.3 (drop never-claimed factors) → 82.4 (CAPM alphas — theory's quantity, and low-beta 'failures' are BAB confirmations) → 75.6 (BY correction) → 82.4 (empirical Bayes, US and global). The zoo is 13 themes; replication holds across the size distribution (mega 77.3%); OOS-vs-IS slopes 0.26–0.57, positive — pure alpha-hacking (slope 0) rejected, though slopes below the 0.90 no-hacking benchmark. Shrinkage: E(α|α̂)=κα̂, κ=1/(1+σ²/(τ²T)) — attenuated OOS alpha is the EXPECTED outcome of learning. Factors BY rejects but Bayes keeps earn IR ≈ 1 afterward.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why does having MORE factors make each individual factor\'s alpha estimate BETTER in JKP\'s model, when HLZ said more factors made everything worse?'

problem_spec.scenario: JKP's posterior: E(α|α̂) = κ·α̂ with κ = 1/(1 + σ²/(τ²T)). A factor has monthly residual vol σ = 2%, prior dispersion τ = 0.4%, T = 100 months, and a reported alpha α̂ = 0.5%/month.
problem_spec.verification: σ²/(τ²T) = 4/(0.16×100) = 4/16 = 0.25. κ = 1/1.25 = 0.80. Posterior alpha = 0.80×0.5 = 0.40%/month. The prior is worth σ²/τ² = 25 months of zero alpha stacked on top of the 100 observed.

slides.title: Real, Replicable — and Tradable?
slides.content_summary: Chen–Welch grant that the anomalies were real and ask what a large-cap manager could have harvested: median long-short return 48bp/mo (through 2005, all stocks) → 26 (cap filter) → 19 (post-2005) → 7bp/mo (both), roughly multiplicative (−85% total); % positive 99→67. Even combining anomalies: 250–380bp gross → 0–20bp net. The four-paper map: HLZ (noise), MP (bias+learning), JKP (replicates), CW (replicates but untradable) — not mutually exclusive; excluded: timing, ML, alt data.

problem_spec.scenario: Chen–Welch medians: 48 bp/month (through 2005, all stocks); 19 bp (post-2005, all stocks); 7 bp (post-2005, top-90% universe).
problem_spec.verification: Era effect alone: (48−19)/48 = 29/48 = 60.4%. Total: (48−7)/48 = 41/48 = 85.4%. Roughly multiplicative with the ~50% cap-filter effect: 0.40×~0.36 ≈ 0.146 ≈ 7/48.

slides.title: Why Theory Is the Cheapest Filter
slides.content_summary: Underfitting vs overfitting; the candidate list includes book-to-price AND the Super Bowl winner AND the position of Mars. Published silliness exists: lunar phases, sports sentiment, temperature. Theory filters noise (price: it also filters unexplained truths — the peso problem cuts both ways). The arithmetic of luck: with 1000 factors tested and 100 real, a t=1.95 screen yields 143 discoveries of which 49 are junk; each extra unit of t costs orders of magnitude more searching, which is why t≥3.0 is the level the field's actual search volume demands.

slides.title: Four Tests, Two Survivors
slides.content_summary: The rule: (1) original t ≥ 3; (2) robustness to specification; (3) out-of-sample in time, countries, asset classes; (4) a sound economic story. VALUE: five constructions all positive (B/P 3.6, E/P 5.3, CF/P 4.5, D/P 1.8, LT-rev 2.5 %/yr; composite 3.5); OOS t: US 3.62, non-US full 4.49, non-US OOS 2.93; two stories. MOMENTUM: 15 of 16 formation×holding constructions clear t=2 (only 3mo/3mo, t 1.10, fails); OOS t: US 2.78, non-US OOS 5.99 — STRONGER abroad out of sample than in; two stories. Both clear all four.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Momentum\'s non-US out-of-sample t (5.99) beats its full-sample t (4.49). Why is that the single most convincing number in the lecture?'

slides.title: Your Turn: Is Value One Lucky Ratio?

problem_spec.scenario: The five value constructions earn (annualized, 1951–2014): B/P 3.6%, E/P 5.3%, CF/P 4.5%, D/P 1.8%, long-term reversal 2.5%. The published composite earns 3.5%.
problem_spec.verification: Mean of the five = (3.6+5.3+4.5+1.8+2.5)/5 = 17.7/5 = 3.54% — essentially the composite's 3.5%: the composite is the average of its parts, not a cherry-pick. Range = 5.3 − 1.8 = 3.5 points: every construction positive, none carrying the result alone.

slides.title: Most Don't Matter — A Few Really Do
slides.content_summary: Citation concentration: Value 72.1k, Size 58.1k, Momentum 33.1k, Beta 19.4k, FSQ 18.3k — roughly 90% of all factor citations in 4–5 factors; on an impact-weighted basis academia focuses on the robust ones. The equal-weighted index of surviving factors has t > 11 — more than a trillion random trials to fluke. The rule to leave the course with: demand t ≥ 3, robustness, out-of-sample evidence, and a story, before you believe a factor exists — and size every position so you survive being wrong.
